title: Past continuous with when and while
tagline: The background action that was happening when something else interrupted it.
why: Good stories need two layers: what was already happening, and what suddenly happened next. In Writing Part 7 that means was/were + -ing for the background, and the past simple for the surprise. Reading and Listening test the same idea: does the sentence need the action in progress, or the shorter one that interrupted it?

hook.text: In Cusco, Liam and Sofia are exploring an old street. Liam was taking photos when it started to rain. "I was walking behind you," says Sofia, "when I slipped!" "Are you OK?" asks Liam.
hook.ask: Two actions here are longer (in progress) and two are shorter (they just happen). Can you find the was/were + -ing forms and match each one to the shorter action that interrupts it?

diagrams.title: An action in progress, interrupted
arrows: the background action was happening when the second one happened
diagrams.caption: The past continuous paints the background; the past simple is the action that happens in the middle of it.

diagrams.title: Build the sentence in the past continuous

parts.t: when the teacher called her name

diagrams.caption: The action in progress uses was/were + -ing; the interrupting action stays in the past simple.

diagrams.title: Adding -ing

rules.rule: Verb ends in -e: drop e + ing
Short verb, one vowel + one consonant: double it
Verb ends in -ie: ie → y + ing

diagrams.caption: Same -ing rules as the present continuous — learn them once, use them for both tenses.

use.point: A background action in progress at a moment in the past

examples.text: At eight o'clock, we were walking to the market.
examples.note: an action in progress at a stated time

examples.text: Sofia was studying at six last night.
Mateo and Liam were playing football at four.
examples.note: were + verb-ing for more than one person

use.point: One action interrupts another — when + past simple

examples.text: Liam was taking photos when it started to rain.
The bus arrived when we were waiting at the stop.
examples.note: the sentence can start with either half

use.point: Two things happening at the same time — while

examples.note: two continuous actions at the same time

examples.text: I was cooking while my brother was doing his homework.
While we were walking, Miss Vega was talking about the Incas.
examples.note: while can start the sentence too

examples.text: I wasn't listening when the teacher called my name.
What were you doing at nine last night?

watch_out.wrong: I walking to school when it started to rain.
watch_out.right: I was walking to school when it started to rain.
watch_out.why: -ing always needs was/were with it — it can't stand alone.

watch_out.wrong: I was seeing a snake and I screamed.
watch_out.right: I saw a snake and I screamed.
watch_out.why: A short, sudden action uses the past simple, not the continuous.

watch_out.wrong: She was runing in the park.
watch_out.why: Short verb, one vowel + one consonant: double the last letter before -ing (run → running).

watch_out.wrong: What you were doing at six?
watch_out.why: In a question, were comes before the person — don't leave it in statement order.

watch_out.wrong: We were walking when we were seeing Machu Picchu.
watch_out.right: We were walking when we saw Machu Picchu.
watch_out.why: The moment you first see something is a short action — use the past simple, not was/were + -ing.

l1.es: Estaba caminando cuando empezó a llover.
l1.wrong: I was walk when it started to rain.
l1.right: I was walking when it started to rain.
l1.why: The continuous always needs the -ing form after was/were — the Spanish gerundio doesn't need this extra helper, so it's easy to forget the -ing.

l1.es: Mientras yo leía, mi hermana dibujaba.
l1.wrong: While I read, my sister drew.
l1.right: While I was reading, my sister was drawing.
l1.why: While usually introduces two actions happening together — English marks that with was/were + -ing on both sides, even though Spanish often just uses the imperfecto.
A quick, one-moment action is past simple, not continuous — don't translate every imperfecto as was/were + -ing.
The question needs were before you, and you always takes were, never was.

remember.trick: Long action + was/were-ing; short action + past simple.
remember.tip: Picture the long action like a video playing in the background — the short action is the photo that interrupts it.

dialogue.title: The rain in Cusco
dialogue.context: Liam and Sofia are on a school trip to Cusco. They are telling Miss Vega what happened during the storm.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Were you two still outside when the storm started?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Yes! I was taking photos of the old street when it started to rain.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: And I was walking behind him when I slipped on the stones!

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: No, I wasn't. Liam was laughing, not helping!

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I wasn't laughing at you — I was laughing because my hat flew away!

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: What were Mateo and Nadia doing at that moment?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: They were waiting under a roof. They weren't in the rain at all.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Lucky them! Next time, check the sky while you are walking.

can_do: I can describe what was happening at a moment in the past with was/were + -ing.
I can join a background action and a shorter action with when and while.
I can make negatives and questions in the past continuous (wasn't listening, What were you doing?).
summary: Past continuous = was/were + -ing, an action in progress at a moment in the past.
It's the background: something longer that was happening when a shorter action (past simple) interrupted it.
When usually introduces the shorter action; while often joins two continuous actions happening together.
The -ing spelling rules are the same ones you use for the present continuous.
